Quick Dollar Drawdown Estimator (2000–2025 Historical Data)

For forty years of falling interest rates, holding 40% in intermediate and long-term bonds reliably cushioned stock declines. The year 2022 exposed the hidden duration flaw inside that classic 60/40 rule: when inflation surges and the Federal Reserve hikes rates rapidly, long-dated bonds lose double digits right alongside equities.

Replacing long-duration bond risk with two distinct defensive tools—non-cyclical healthcare equity cash flows (XLV) and ultra-short 0–3 month Treasury bills (SGOV)—removed duration shock from the defensive side of the ledger.

While short-term T-bills yield less during near-zero rate regimes, their near-zero duration means principal stays intact when rates jump, keeping household cash ready exactly when market stress peaks.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did SGOV stay positive in 2022 while AGG and TLT fell sharply?

SGOV holds US Treasury bills maturing in 0 to 3 months, so rising Federal Reserve rates reset its yield higher almost immediately instead of crushing bond prices.

Is 60/40 obsolete for every saver?

Not necessarily; bonds still play a role in many balanced plans. Our research simply lays out the 25-year numbers side by side so self-directed readers can see how duration behaved in 2022.
